title: High-Fidelity Entangled States in a Connectivity-Four Fluxonium Quantum Processor
authors: J. Schirk, N. Bruckmoser, S. M. Taubenberger, F. Wallner, N. J. Glaser, M. Zetzl, L. Huang, I. Tsitsilin, M. Werninghaus, L. Södergren, K. Liegener, C. M. F. Schneider, Stefan Filipp
abstract: A central challenge in fluxonium-based quantum processors is the extension of the qubit connectivity to two-dimensional lattices compatible with quantum code-error correction. Here, we present a fluxonium quantum processor that employs lumped-element resonator couplers which realizes, for the first time, a connectivity-four unit cell with suppressed parasitic interactions. We achieve parallel single-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.9 % in simultaneous randomized benchmarking experiments, while maintaining residual static ZZ interactions below 1 kHz across all coupled qubit pairs. We implement resonator-induced phase (RIP) gates and benchmark two-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99 % using interleaved randomized benchmarking. To cancel spectator errors observed in two-qubit operations, we implement a refocused RIP gate, recovering coherent control in the presence of multi-qubit connectivity. Furthermore, we prepare Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states of up to five qubits with a tomographic fidelity of 90 %, verifying multi-qubit entanglement within the unit cell. These results establish the fluxonium-resonator-fluxonium architecture as a viable approach to realizing densely connected fluxonium processors and provide a scalable path toward quantum error-correction-compatible processor architectures.
summary: This paper reports the realization of a high-connectivity (connectivity-four) quantum processor using fluxonium qubits coupled via resonators. The authors achieved state-of-the-art gate fidelities and demonstrated robust multi-qubit entanglement preparation. This establishes the fluxonium-resonator-fluxonium architecture as a viable, scalable path toward error-correction-compatible quantum hardware.
main_problem: The central challenge is extending qubit connectivity to two-dimensional lattices for quantum error correction in fluxonium processors while suppressing parasitic interactions.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a connectivity-four unit cell using a fluxonium-resonator-fluxonium architecture, achieving high-fidelity single-qubit gates (>99.9%) and controlled two-qubit gates (>99%).
method: Gate fidelities were measured using randomized benchmarking (RB/IRB), and multi-qubit entanglement was verified by preparing and measuring GHZ states via quantum state tomography.
model_or_system: The system uses fluxonium qubits coupled via lumped-element resonator couplers, realizing a connectivity-four unit cell. The Hamiltonian includes terms for qubits and the resonator, with coupling mediated by state-dependent dispersive shifts.
key_observables: Single-qubit gate fidelities, two-qubit gate fidelities, GHZ state tomographic fidelity, and residual static ZZ interactions.
important_parameters: Single-qubit fidelity > 99.9%; Two-qubit fidelity > 99%; Residual ZZ interaction < 1 kHz; Connectivity = 4.
main_assumptions: The coupling strategy relies on exploiting selection rules at the lower sweet-spot where even-numbered transitions are forbidden.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the chip architecture, showing the FRF coupling scheme and the spectral diagram of dispersive shifts. Other figures detail fidelity measurements and error mitigation protocols.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the connectivity-four architecture, details the Hamiltonian and coupling mechanism, presents experimental results for single-qubit and two-qubit gates, and concludes by validating multi-qubit entanglement preparation.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses scalable hardware implementation for quantum computation, providing concrete metrics (high fidelity, controlled connectivity) for superconducting qubit platforms relevant to quantum error correction.

FIG. 3. Spectator error mitigation. (a) Configuration of a regular RIP gate between two qubits q1 and q5 with no operation on the spectator qubit q2 results in a spectator state-dependent error when q2 is in |1⟩, as characterized by IRB (c). The gate is calibrated for the case where q2 is in |0⟩. (b) Refocusing RIP gate. The RIP pulse is split into two sections, split by a π-pulse on q2, resulting in a cancellation of conditional phases caused by the spectator qubit and no dependence of the CZ-gate fidelity in IRB (d).
